segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: What I am saying is this: as long as the heir is a minor, he is no different from a slave, though he is master of everything,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: but he is under guardians and managers until the date set by his father.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So it was with us too: when we were minors, we were enslaved under the elements of the world.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But when the fullness of time came, God sent his Son, born of a woman, born under law,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: to redeem those under law, so that we might receive adoption as sons.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And because you are sons, God sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying out,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Abba, Father!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So you are no longer a slave but a son; and if a son, then also an heir through God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But back then, not knowing God, you were slaves to things that by nature are not gods.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now, though, you have come to know God, or rather to be known by God. How can you turn back again to the weak and impoverished elements? Do you want to be their slaves all over again?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: You are observing days and months and seasons and years!

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I am afraid for you, that somehow I may have labored over you for nothing.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Become as I am, because I too have become as you are, brothers and sisters; I beg you. You did me no wrong.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: You know that it was because of a bodily illness that I proclaimed the good news to you at first,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and what was a trial to you in my body you did not scorn or spit at; instead you welcomed me as an angel of God, as Christ Jesus.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So where is that blessedness of yours now? For I testify to you that, if it had been possible, you would have dug out your eyes and given them to me.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So have I become your enemy by telling you the truth?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They are courting you, but not in a good way; they want to shut you out, so that you will court them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now it is always good to be courted in a good way, and not only when I am present with you,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: my children, with whom I am in labor again until Christ is formed in you.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I wish I could be present with you now and change my tone, because I am at a loss about you.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Tell me, you who want to be under law, do you not listen to the law?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For it is written that Abraham had two sons, one by the slave woman and one by the free woman.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But the one by the slave woman was born according to the flesh, while the one by the free woman was born through a promise.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: These things are spoken allegorically, for these women are two covenants. One is from Mount Sinai, bearing children into slavery; this is Hagar.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now Hagar is Mount Sinai in Arabia, and she corresponds to the present Jerusalem, for she is in slavery with her children.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But the Jerusalem above is free, and she is our mother.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For it is written:

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “Rejoice, barren woman who bears no children; break out and shout, you who are not in labor; for the children of the desolate woman are many, more than those of the woman who has a husband.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now you, brothers and sisters, are children of promise, like Isaac.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But just as at that time the one born according to the flesh persecuted the one born according to the Spirit, so it is now as well.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But what does the scripture say?

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “Throw out the slave woman and her son, for the son of the slave woman will certainly not inherit along with the son of the free woman.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Therefore, brothers and sisters, we are not children of a slave woman but of the free woman.

notes.traditional: elements of the world; elementary principles of the world; elemental spirits of the world
notes.note: The Greek word meant the basic components of something: letters of the alphabet, the rudiments of a subject, and most often in this period the physical elements (earth, water, air, fire) of which the world was thought to be made. Translations divide between "elementary principles" (basic religious rules) and "elemental spirits" (cosmic powers), though use of the word for spirits is not clearly attested this early. The plain rendering is kept so as not to settle a disputed question. Verses 8–10 connect these elements both with pagan gods and with calendar observance.

notes.traditional: adoption as sons; the adoption of sons
notes.note: This is the ordinary legal term for adoption, which in the Greco-Roman world usually meant making someone, often an adult male, one's legal heir. "Sons" is kept in verses 5–7 because the argument turns on inheritance and on sharing the status of God's own Son. Paul has just said (3:28) that this status belongs to male and female alike.

Abba is the Aramaic word for "father", used in addressing one's own father by children and adults alike. Paul gives the Aramaic followed by its Greek equivalent, as in Romans 8:15. Mark 14:36 records Jesus praying with the same double address.

notes.traditional: an heir of God through Christ
notes.note: Many later manuscripts read "an heir of God through Christ", the wording behind the King James Version. The earliest witnesses have the shorter and more unusual "through God", which scribes appear to have expanded into more familiar phrasing.

The Greek plural was the normal way to address a mixed group of men and women as siblings, and Paul is writing to whole congregations. "Brothers" alone would suggest to a modern reader that only men are addressed. Several current translations make the same choice.

notes.traditional: infirmity of the flesh; a bodily ailment
notes.note: Literally "a weakness of the flesh". The word commonly means illness and most interpreters take it so here, but it could refer to physical weakness of another kind, such as the effects of injuries. What the condition was is not known. "At first" can also be read as "the first time", which would imply that Paul had visited the Galatians twice.

The verb literally means "spit out". Spitting was a familiar gesture both of contempt and of warding off illness or evil, and a first-century reader would probably have heard both. Most translations paraphrase with "reject" or "despise"; the concrete image is kept here.

notes.traditional: zealously affect; make much of; are zealous for
notes.note: The verb means to be zealous about someone or to pursue them eagerly, here of rival teachers seeking the Galatians' allegiance. "Court" allows one English word for all three occurrences in verses 17–18, preserving Paul's play on the word. What the Galatians are to be "shut out" from is not stated; most take it to be fellowship with Paul, or full standing among God's people unless they adopt the law.

The Greek verb can mean either to speak in allegory or to interpret something allegorically. Paul may be saying that the Genesis story itself carries a further meaning, or simply that he is now reading it that way. Scholars disagree, and the rendering leans slightly toward the first.

notes.phrase: Now Hagar is Mount Sinai in Arabia
notes.traditional: For this Agar is mount Sinai in Arabia
notes.note: The manuscripts differ here. Some read "For Sinai is a mountain in Arabia", without the name Hagar, and there are other variations. The translation follows the SBLGNT text. Why Paul links Hagar with Sinai is not explained and remains uncertain; on either reading his point is that Hagar belongs with the Sinai covenant.

Genesis 21:9 says only that Sarah saw Hagar's son "playing", and the Greek version adds "with her son Isaac". Some Jewish interpretation understood this as mockery or hostile behaviour, and Paul appears to read the story that way.

notes.phrase: “Throw out the slave woman and her son, for the son of the slave woman will certainly not inherit along with the son of the free woman.”
notes.traditional: Cast out the bondwoman and her son
notes.note: These are Sarah's words to Abraham in Genesis 21:10, which Paul cites as the voice of scripture. He adapts the ending: Genesis has "with my son Isaac", for which Paul writes "with the son of the free woman" to fit his contrast.

candidates.reason: It recurs in Galatians 4, Colossians 2, Hebrews 5 and 2 Peter 3, and translations vary between elements, elementary principles and elemental spirits, which obscures the links between the passages.
The plural address is pervasive in the letters and Acts, and the choice between "brothers" and "brothers and sisters" needs to be uniform.
The word means both covenant and will or testament, and Galatians 3:15–17 and Hebrews 9:15–18 play on both senses, so a single policy is needed.
Paul's range runs from the physical body to natural descent to the sphere opposed to the Spirit, and when to keep "flesh" needs one consistent rule.
It occurs five times in Paul, and translations vary between adoption, adoption as sons, adoption as children and sonship.
